name: No Name on the Ledger (Shelf Sending)
description:
Written in 2196 by Amara Kofi-Lindgren, a Shelf-born singer who lost three family members to a single winter of infrastructure failures, 'No Name on the Ledger (Shelf Sending)' is the standard funeral song for Tier 1 communities across GLMZ. It addresses directly the reality of Shelf death: that many who die in the lowest tier are never officially recorded, their deaths attributed to system errors or left uncategorized in databases that corporate interests have no reason to maintain accurately. The song is a ceremony of naming — the singer calls out the names of the dead, slowly, and the gathered mourners respond with a single sustained tone, a drone rooted in North African funerary tradition but long since absorbed into the Shelf's own ritual life. The melody is simple enough to be sung without rehearsal, in any key, by people who have never met before this moment.

The song has no fixed verses — the community inserts the names of their specific dead into the structure, and the only fixed lines are the frame: 'they kept no name on the ledger / but we keep yours in the mouth / we keep yours in the bone / we keep yours in the ground.' Kofi-Lindgren has said she did not copyright the song and never will, that it belongs to everyone who needs it. Vantablack-aligned media companies have attempted twice to register variations of the melody for commercial use, and both times Shelf communities organized public responses so intense that the registrations were quietly withdrawn.
creator: Amara Kofi-Lindgren
genre: Shelf funeral tradition, communal drone, mourning folk
audience: Tier 1 communities primarily, Tier 2 working-class communities, anyone from the lower tiers who has lost someone to institutional neglect or uncounted death, labor communities, Shelf elders and grief leaders
cultural_impact: The song has become the de facto funeral rite for communities that cannot afford formal services and whose dead are not counted by official systems. It functions as both grief ritual and political act — the act of naming the unnamed is understood by everyone present as a form of resistance. Civil rights organizations have used recordings of mass singings of the song as evidence in legal cases arguing for improved death-recording requirements in Tier 1 zones. The song is taught to Shelf children early, not as something morbid, but as something necessary — the understanding that your community will remember you even if the system does not.
known_fans: Shelf community elders and grief leaders
Tier 2 workers who grew up on the Shelf
story_hooks: The players attend a Shelf funeral where the community is singing this song for someone who, according to every corporate database, does not exist — but who the community insists was real, was known, and was killed for something they knew.

Amara Kofi-Lindgren is being pressured by a Vantablack subsidiary to sign a contract that would give them commercial rights to the song's melody in exchange for financial security — and community leaders are asking the players to help her find an alternative before she's forced to choose.

A mass singing of the song is being organized in a public space as a political demonstration, and someone has tipped off corporate security — the players need to decide whether to help protect the gathering, infiltrate the security operation, or get out of the way.
